edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 1, Paris 1844), De baptismo, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Sed si certaminis nomine Deus nobis martyria proposuisset, per quae cum adversario experiremur, ut a quo libenter homo elisus est, eum jam constanter elidat, hic quoque liberalitas magis, quam acerbitas Dei praeest. Evulsum enim hominem de diaboli gula per fidem, jam et inculcatorem ejus voluit efficere per virtutem; ne solummodo evasisset, verum etiam evicisset inimicum. Amavit, qui vocaverat in salutem, invitare et ad gloriam; ut gaudeamus liberati, exultemus etiam coronati. Agonas istos, contentiosa solemnia et superstitiosa certamina graecarum et religionum et voluptatum, quanta gratia saeculum celebret, etiam Africae liquit. Adhuc Carthaginem singulae civitates gratulando inquietant, donatam pythico agone post stadii senectutem. Ita ab aevo dignissimum creditum est stadiorum experimentum, committere artes, corporum et vocum praestantiam exprimere, praemio indice, spectaculo judice, sententia voluptate: qua nulla sunt praelia, non nulla vulnera, pugni quassant, calces arietant, cestus dilaniant, flagella dilacerant: nemo tamen agonis praesidem suggillaverit, quod homines violentiae objectat, injuriarum actiones extra stadium, sed quantum livores illi et cruores et vibices negotiantur intendet: coronas scilicet, et gloriam, et dotem, privilegia publica, stipendia civica, imagines, statuas, et qualem potest praestare saeculum de fama aeternitatem, de memoria resurrectionem. Pyctes ipse non queritur dolere se, nam vult, corona premit vulnera, palma sanguinem obscurat; plus victoria tumet quam injuria. Hunc tu laesum existimabis, quem vides laetum? Sed nec victus ipse de agonotheta casum suum exprobrabit. Deum dedecebit artes et disciplinas suas educere in medium, in hoc saeculi spatium, in spectaculum hominibus et angelis et universis potestatibus? carnem atque animam probare de constantia atque tolerantia? dare huic palmam, huic honorem, illi civitatem, illi stipendia? etiam quosdam reprobare, et castigatos cum ignominia summovere? Nimirum praescribes Deo, quibus temporibus, aut modis, aut locis de familia sua judicet, quasi non et praejudicare judici congruat. Quid nunc, si non certaminis nomine in martyria fidem exposuisset, sed et proprii profectus; nonne oportebat illam habere aliquem spei cumulum, cui studium suum cogeret, votumque suspenderet, quo eniteretur ascendere, cum terrena quoque officia in gradus aestuent? aut quomodo multae mansiones apud Patrem, si non pro varietate meritorum? quomodo et stella a stella distabit in gloria, nisi pro diversitate radiorum? Porro, et si fidei propterea congruebat sublimitatis et claritatis aliqua prolatio, tale quid esse oportuerat illud emolumenti, quod magno constaret labore, cruciatu, tormento, morte. Sed respice compensationem: cum caro et anima dependitur, quibus in homine carius nihil est; alterum manus Dei, alterum flatus; ipsa dependi in profectu, quorum est profectus; ipsa erogari, quae lucrifiant; eadem pretia, quae et merces. Prospexerat et has Deus imbecillitates conditionis humanae, adversarii insidias, rerum fallacias, saeculi retia, etiam post lavacrum periclitaturam fidem, perituros plerosque rursum post salutem, qui vestitum obsoletassent nuptialem, qui faculis oleum non praeparassent, qui requirendi per montes et saltus, et humeris essent reportandi. Posuit igitur secunda solatia, extrema praesidia, dimicationem martyrii, et lavacrum sanguinis exinde securum. De cujus felicitate David: Beati quorum dimissa sunt delicta, et quorum opertae sunt iniquitates. Beatus vir cui non imputaverit Deus delictum. Proprie enim martyribus nihil jam reputari potest, quibus in lavacro ipsa vita deponitur. Sic dilectio operit multitudinem delictorum, quae Deum scilicet diligens ex totis viribus suis, quibus in martyrio decertat, ex tota anima sua, quam pro Deo ponit, hominem martyrem excudit. Haec tu remedia, consilia, judicia, spectacula etiam Dei atrocitatem judicabis? sanguinem hominis Deus concupiscit? Et tamen ausim dicere, si et homo regnum Dei, si homo certam salutem, si et homo secundam regenerationem. Nulli compensatio invidiosa est, in qua aut gratiae, aut injuriae communis est ratio.
pass_a_gloss: But if God had proposed to us martyrdoms by the name of a contest, through which we would experience with an adversary, so that the one from whom a person is gladly freed, he may now constantly overcome, even in this case the liberality of God is more evident than His harshness. For God willed that a person torn away from the devil's jaws through faith would also become his conqueror through virtue, so that he would not only have escaped but also have overcome the enemy. He who loved, and who had called to salvation, also willed to invite to glory, so that we may rejoice having been freed, and also exult having been crowned. Those agonistic contests, contentious and superstitious ceremonies of the Greeks, and of religions, and of pleasures, which the world celebrates with so much gratitude, even Africa has abandoned. Still, individual cities disturb Carthage by congratulating it, having been given the Pythian contest after the old age of the stadium. Thus, from ancient times it has been considered most worthy to commit the arts to the stadium, to express the excellence of bodies and voices, with a prize as the indicator, a spectacle as the judge, and a sentence as pleasure. In these contests, there are no battles, but there are many wounds: blows shatter, kicks strike, fists tear, whips lacerate. Nevertheless, no one has ever reproached the guardian of the contest, because men object to violence, and actions of injury take place outside the stadium, but as for the bruises, and the blood, and the welts that are negotiated, they are intended for: crowns, glory, dowry, public privileges, civic stipends, images, statues, and the kind of eternity of fame, and resurrection of memory that the world can provide. The boxer himself does not complain of being in pain, for he wants to, the crown presses upon his wounds, the palm obscures his blood; the victory swells more than the injury. Will you consider this man to be injured, whom you see to be joyful? But neither will the defeated man himself reproach the judge of the contest for his fall. Will God be ashamed to bring forth His arts and disciplines into the midst, into this space of the world, into a spectacle for men and angels and all powers? to test flesh and soul for constancy and tolerance? to give the palm to this one, honor to that one, citizenship to another, stipends to another? and also to reject some, and to remove the chastised with ignominy? You are surely prescribing to God the times, or the ways, or the places in which He should judge His own family, as if it were not fitting for a judge to prejudge. What now, if God had not exposed faith to martyrdom by the name of a contest, but also for its own progress? Was it not necessary for it to have some accumulation of hope, to which its zeal would be drawn, and its vow would be suspended, by which it would strive to ascend, since even earthly offices are esteemed in grades? Or how are there many dwellings with the Father, if not according to the variety of merits? How does a star differ from a star in glory, if not according to the diversity of rays? Furthermore, if it were fitting for faith to have some prolongation of sublimity and clarity, it was necessary for that benefit to be such that it would consist of great labor, torture, torment, death. But look at the compensation: when flesh and soul are at stake, which are more precious to man than anything else; one is the hand of God, the other the breath of God; these very things are at stake in progress, whose progress they are; these very things are expended, which bring gain; the same prices, which are also rewards. God has also foreseen these weaknesses of the human condition, the snares of the adversary, the deceptions of things, the snares of the world, and even after baptism, faith will be in danger, and most people will perish again after salvation, who have worn out their wedding garment, who have not prepared oil for their lamps, who will have to be sought out over mountains and hills, and will have to be carried on shoulders. Therefore, God has established second comforts, extreme aids, the struggle of martyrdom, and the baptism of blood, which is henceforth secure. Concerning the happiness of which David says: Blessed are those whose sins are forgiven, and whose iniquities are covered. Blessed is the man to whom God does not impute sin. For martyrs, indeed, nothing can be imputed, to whom life itself is laid down in the baptism. Thus, love covers a multitude of sins, which, of course, he who loves God with all his strength, with which he struggles in martyrdom, with his whole soul, which he lays down for God, the martyr is formed. Will you judge these remedies, counsels, judgments, and even spectacles to be the cruelty of God? Does God covet the blood of man? And yet I dare to say, if man is the kingdom of God, if man is certain salvation, if man is also second regeneration. No compensation is envied, in which the reason of either grace or injury is common.

pass_b_english: Suppose God had offered us martyrdoms under the label of a contest, matches in which we would prove ourselves against an adversary, so that the very one from whom a person is gladly freed he might now steadily conquer; even then God's generosity would outweigh his severity. He wanted the human being ripped from the devil's jaws by faith to become the devil's conqueror by virtue, so that he would not merely escape but actually defeat the enemy. The One who loved us and called us to salvation also chose to invite us to glory, that we might rejoice in our liberation and exult in our crowning. Those brutal games—contentious, superstitious rites of the Greeks, of religions, of pleasures—which the world celebrates with such enthusiasm, even Africa has abandoned. Yet individual cities still harass Carthage with congratulations because she was awarded the Pythian games after the stadium's heyday had passed. From ancient times it was deemed supremely worthwhile to commit the arts to the stadium, to display the excellence of bodies and voices, with a prize as the measure, a spectacle as the judge, and pleasure as the verdict. In these contests there are no battles, yet wounds abound: blows shatter, kicks hammer, fists tear, whips lacerate. Still, no one ever reproaches the games' overseer, even though men decry violence and lawsuits for injury arise outside the arena; they only calculate how many bruises, how much blood, how many welts can be traded for crowns, glory, dowries, public privileges, civic stipends, images, statues, and the kind of eternal fame and resurrection of memory the world can supply. The boxer himself does not complain of pain, because he chooses it; the crown presses down his wounds, the palm obscures his blood; victory swells more than injury. Will you call that man injured whom you see rejoicing? Nor will the loser himself reproach the judge for his fall. Would God be ashamed to bring his arts and disciplines into the open, into this world's arena, into a spectacle for men and angels and all powers—to test flesh and soul for constancy and endurance, to award the palm to one, honor to another, citizenship to another, stipends to another, and also to reject some and dismiss the chastised in disgrace? You are effectively dictating to God the times, manners, and places in which he may judge his own household, as if a judge ought not to prejudge. What if God had not exposed faith to martyrdom under the name of a contest, but for its own advance? Would it not need some store of hope to draw its zeal and anchor its vow, the means by which it strives to ascend, since even earthly offices are ranked in grades? How else are there many dwellings with the Father, if not according to the variety of merits? How does one star differ from another in glory, if not by the diversity of its rays? (1 Corinthians 15:41). Moreover, if faith required some extension of sublimity and clarity, that benefit had to be one purchased by great labor, torture, torment, death. But consider the compensation: when flesh and soul are at stake—the two things dearer to a human being than anything else; one is the hand of God, the other the breath of God—these very things are ventured in the advance that belongs to them; these very things are spent, which bring gain; the same prices that are also rewards. God foresaw these frailties of the human condition, the adversary's snares, the deceptions of things, the world's nets, and that even after baptism faith would be endangered, that most would perish again after salvation—those who have worn out their wedding garment, who have not prepared oil for their lamps, who must be sought over mountains and hills and carried back on shoulders (Matthew 22:11-13; 25:1-13; Luke 15:4-5). Therefore he provided second comforts, final defenses, the struggle of martyrdom, and the baptism of blood, thereafter secure. Of its blessedness David says: "Blessed are those whose transgressions are forgiven, whose sins are covered. Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord does not count against them" (Psalm 32:1-2). For martyrs, indeed, nothing can be imputed, since life itself is laid down in that baptism. Thus love covers a multitude of sins (1 Peter 4:8)—the love of the one who loves God with all his strength, with which he wrestles in martyrdom, with his whole soul, which he lays down for God; the martyr is forged. Will you pronounce these remedies, counsels, judgments, and even spectacles to be the cruelty of God? Does God crave human blood? And yet I dare say: if man is the kingdom of God, if man is certain salvation, if man is also a second regeneration, no compensation is envied when the rationale of either grace or injury is shared.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful literal rendering, and Pass B provides a fluent rendering that correctly identifies and adds the necessary scripture citations (1 Corinthians 15:41, Matthew 22:11-13, 25:1-13, Luke 15:4-5, Psalm 32:1-2, and 1 Peter 4:8) which correspond to the Latin allusions/quotes. All clauses, including the complex theological arguments regarding the 'compensation' and the 'second comforts', are preserved.
